# Simulation framework

This thesis uses an acceptance loop which has been further developed
from the loop described in @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL. In this section the
components of the loop are defined, i.e.

- The joint distribution $\mathbb{P}_{(Y, X)}$ of the repayment variable
  and the covariates,
- the acceptance decision $Z^{(t)}$ for each acceptance round, meaning formulating
    - the estimation method of the score function $s_t$,
    - the threshold calculation and
    - the complete decision function $d$ for both the MAR and MNAR cases
- from which the rest of the RVs and functions get formulated.

After defining each of the components an overview of the process as an algorithm
is provided.

## Applicants' population {#sec-app-population-simulation}

Recalling section @sec-measure-theoretic-desc-ri-problem, according to
the probabilistic model for the RL problem it suffices to define the
distributions of the repayment outcome and the features to define the applicants'
population. In this thesis I do not consider latent features (case $f_l = 0$).
Further let $\tilde{Y} := Y | \{\epsilon = \text{no external effect}\}$ denote
the "noiseless" repayment outcome. I describe the population with this variable,
since it is less convoluted, is the object that the scorecard will
attempt to model and is easily bridged to the idea of a good and bad applicants.
It holds $\tilde{Y} \sim Bernoulli(\pi_{b})$ with $\pi_b \in (0,1)$
the probability of a bad applicant. The observable features vector $X$^[
    Recall from @eq-X-joint-observable-feats-vec: $X = \begin{pmatrix}X_m \\ X_h \end{pmatrix}$
]
is defined as a Gaussian Mixture with two components, a good one (paying population)
and a bad one (defaulters). With $o \in \{g, b\}$ we can characterize the distributions
of these populations as
$$
X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(
    \mu_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \mu_{m, o} \\ \mu_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix},
    \Sigma_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \Sigma_{m, o} & \Sigma_{mh, o} \\
        \Sigma_{mh, o}^{\top} & \Sigma_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix}
\right)
$$
with $\Sigma, \Sigma_{m, o}$ and $\Sigma_{h, o}$ strictly positive definite (so, non-singular).
Letting $X_o$ be short for $X | \{Y=o\}$ also let $\phi_{X_o}$ denote its probability density
function (pdf). Since $X_o$ is normally distributed the pdf is given by
$$
\phi_{X_o}(x) := 
\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^f |\Sigma_o|} }
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)\right\}
$$

For further analysis it is also helpful to write down the characterization of the joint distribution
of $(X,\tilde{Y})$ namely^[
    The regularity and existence of this distribution follows from the fact that the
    conditional kernel of $\mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, Y}$ exists (as discussed in the
    footnote after @eq-joint-dist-feats-and-repayment). Since $\varepsilon$ is
    sigma finite as well the regularity conditions are passed to 
    $\mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, \tilde{Y}}$
]
$$
\mathbb{P}_{X, \tilde{Y}} := \int_{\mathbb{R}^{f_l}} \mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, Y} \, d \mathbb{P}_{X_l} \, .
$$

Its density^[
    A small note on formalism based on @Pollard_2001 [Ch. 3, Sec. 1]: often in the literature densities
    are only defined for "continuous RVs", meaning RVs with distributions absolutely continuous
    with respect to Lebesgue measure. Therefore, it might seem unnatural to say that $(X, Y)$ has
    a density when $\mathbb{P}_Y$ is not absolutely continuous w. r. t. Lebesgue. However, from a
    measure theoretic perspective we only need absolute continuity to some other measure, in this
    case a probability measure defined over the product space
    $\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f} \right) \otimes 2^{E_y}$.
] is a map $\mathbb{R} \times E_y \to [0, 1]$ given by
$$
p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) = \pi_o \cdot \phi_{X_o}(x)
$$
where $\phi_{X_o}$ is the probability density function (pdf)
of the multivariate normal distribution of $X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\}$ and $\pi_g := 1 - \pi_b$.

From this we can easily derive the marginals
$$
p_\tilde{Y}(o) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{f}} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) \, \mathbb{P}_{X}(dx) = \pi_o ,
$$
which of course corresponds to the probability mass function of a Bernoulli
distributed variable, and
$$
p_X(x) = \int_{E_Y} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, y) \, \mathbb{P}_{\tilde{Y}}(dy) = \pi_b \phi_{X_b}(x) + \pi_g \phi_{X_g}(x)
$$

From this describing the density of the distribution $Y | X$ is straightforward^[
    Again remember the note on regularity of the conditional probability kernels
    of $\mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, \tilde{Y}}$, which implies here the existence of the
    respective densities with a similar argument as the last note (integrability
    is ensured). Theorem 12 from @Pollard_2001 [Ch. 4] applies, where the regularity
    condition on the denominator is assured by the normal nature of the components and
    by $\pi_b \notin \{0, 1\}$.
]
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y} = o | X=x) \equiv \frac{\mathbb{P}(X = x | \tilde{Y}=o) \, \mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y}=o)}{\mathbb{P}(X = x)}
$$
which can be written in terms of the densities above:
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y} = o | X=x) = p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (o, x) = \frac{\phi_{X_o}(x) p_\tilde{Y}(o)}{p_X(x)}
$$
